claims.text: Laser cladding of the proposed composite coating can repair damaged 316L stainless-steel surfaces.
Conventional fusion-welding repair creates a hot-cracking risk in the specified 316L components.
FeCoNiCrMo0.2 coatings containing WC and nano-CeO2 can be deposited on 316L stainless steel by laser cladding.
The proposed laser cladding uses optimized low-power or low-heat-input parameters.
The proposed laser cladding is conducted under an inert-gas atmosphere.
Laser cladding has fast heating and cooling characteristics.
The coating can be laser-cladded while remaining below fusion-melting temperatures and retaining a solid-state microstructure.
Nano-CeO2 refines the grain structure of the FeCoNiCrMo0.2-WC coating.
The resulting coating contains uniformly dispersed WC reinforcement.
WC reinforcement and CeO2-induced grain refinement reduce residual stresses and mitigate hot-crack formation.
Rapid solidification minimizes thermal input and residual-stress buildup during laser cladding.
Adding WC increases the hardness of the FeCoNiCrMo0.2 coating.
Adding WC improves the coating's wear-related performance by reducing its friction factor.
The FeCoNiCrMo0.2-WC-CeO2 coating has enhanced corrosion resistance, including higher polarization impedance and a lower corrosion rate.
The laser-cladded surface will have higher hardness and better wear and corrosion resistance than traditional fusion-weld repairs.
The laser-cladded surface will have higher hardness and better wear and corrosion resistance than untreated 316L stainless steel.
The laser-cladded surface will exhibit minimal hot cracking.
The composite coating is suitable for service involving both high wear and corrosive conditions.
Performance is bounded by surface geometry and by controlled processing temperatures and cooling rates.
Failure to achieve statistically significant improvements over both controls, or observing similar or increased hot-crack incidence, would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The intervention is described as laser cladding with rapid solidification, but the conditions and boundary require temperatures below fusion melting and maintenance of a solid-state microstructure. Solidification presupposes prior melting, so these process descriptions are internally incompatible.
